lines.text: The word RAM charged one step for any memory access. Once the vector outgrows memory, what you pay for is blocks moved, and the count changes completely.
Here is our vector again, grown to a gigabyte of sixty four bit keys. It no longer fits in the memory the program is given.
So every touch might mean something travelling in from disk. Watch what that does to the arithmetic.

tolerated.line: So every touch might mean something travelling in from disk. Watch what that does to the arithmetic.

lines.text: Before we count anything, commit to a guess. Visit a million keys of this vector.
First in sorted order, in one sweep. Then in random order, jumping around.
The disk moves data in blocks of five hundred and twelve keys.
Which visit moves fewer blocks, and by how much?
The sweep costs about five hundred and twelve times fewer transfers.
In a sweep, five hundred and twelve keys arrive together, so you pay one transfer per block. A random visit lands every key in its own block, so you pay about one per key.
The same work, a factor of five hundred apart. Saying they cost about the same, or that random is cheaper, ignores that a block is delivered whole.
That gap is the whole reason we need a new cost model.
Here is the model, from Aggarwal and Vitter, nineteen eighty eight. Look at its shape: two levels.
A fast memory that holds M items, and a slow store that only ever moves whole blocks of B items.
Everything you do to data already in memory is free. That sounds like cheating, but it is the honest simplification when a block costs more than thousands of comparisons.
The meter runs only when a block crosses the boundary.
Three numbers describe any job. N is the items in the problem. M is the items that fit in memory. B is the items in one block.
For our gigabyte vector, read the values off the screen. N is a hundred and thirty four million keys, and the whole vector is just sixteen memory loads long.
Hold onto that sixteen. It is going to decide how the sort finishes.

tolerated.line: Hold onto that sixteen. It is going to decide how the sort finishes.

lines.text: The simplest operation is a scan, reading every item once.
Each block is touched exactly once, in order. So the cost is N over B, about two hundred and sixty thousand transfers, all sequential.
That number is a floor. Nothing that must read all the data can beat it, which is why every other bound is measured against it.
Now searching one key among sorted keys. On the word RAM, binary search costs log base two of N, here twenty seven probes.
But look at what one transfer buys you now. A whole block of keys arrives, so it rules out all but one of B equal slices of the range.
So the search costs log base B of N: three reads instead of twenty seven.
A binary tree wastes the block. A tree whose nodes are blocks, which is a B tree, uses all of it. We come back to that in a later chapter.

tolerated.line: A binary tree wastes the block. A tree whose nodes are blocks, which is a B tree, uses all of it. We come back to that in a later chapter.

lines.text: Sorting next. Fill memory, sort what is there in place, and write it out as a sorted run. Then merge runs together.
Do the arithmetic from the numbers you already hold. The vector is sixteen memory loads long, and memory holds sixteen thousand blocks.
How many passes, total?
Two.
The first pass writes sixteen sorted runs. One merge can swallow up to sixteen thousand runs at once, so sixteen is nothing, and a single merge finishes the job.
Run formation, then one merge. One pass would need the whole vector in memory, and sixteen or four passes assume a far smaller fan in than memory gives.
That is where the famous sort bound comes from. Read the logarithm in it as a count of passes.
Each merge holds one block from about M over B runs in memory at once, so every pass divides the number of runs by that fan in.
And the fan in is in the thousands. A two way merge of the same runs would need four passes instead of one.
Comparisons gave us a log in base two. Blocks give us a log in base M over B. The base is the memory.
Step back and count the same sort twice.
By comparisons it is billions. By block transfers it is about half a million, the two scans from before.
In practice the stopwatch tracks the transfers, since one block off a disk costs more than thousands of comparisons in memory.
That is the lesson of the model: once data lives out of memory, bytes moved decide the cost, not operations counted.
This also pays a debt from the amortized chapter. We proved the doubling vector costs one write per append on balance. What is that in blocks?
A resize copies the contents, and a copy is a scan. Add up every resize: fewer than two N items copied in total.
So at most about two N over B transfers, which is about one over B of a transfer per append.
The amortized proof and the block model agree, and the bound only got stronger.
One more gift: this is the same model at every level of the machine.
At the disk, a block is a page of five hundred and twelve keys. At the processor, a block is a cache line, just eight keys, and M becomes the cache.
Only M and B change. The counting is identical.
So the next time a loop is slow, ask which boundary its blocks are crossing.
Now test the model on a design choice. A hash table too big for memory, with N records, and you probe every one of them in turn.
Compare it against sorting the table first and sweeping it once.
How do the transfer counts compare?
About N transfers for the lookups, since each lands in its own block.
Sorting first costs only a couple of passes of about N over B. So sorting wins by a factor close to B.
Neither is cheaper just because lookups are fewer. The count depends on B, and that is why external engines sort or partition before they probe.
Hold N and B fixed, and let the data grow far past memory.
Think about what has to change for the sort to need a third pass.
Is two passes a ceiling the sort will outgrow, or does it hold forever?
It does grow, but it stays small for a very long way.
The pass count ticks up only when the number of runs, N over M, first exceeds the fan in, M over B.
That is the moment memory starts to matter, long after the data stopped fitting in it. Two forever and growing with every doubling are both wrong, and B alone does not decide it.

lines.text: Last, an honest caveat. The model counts transfers. It does not give you nanoseconds.
Device latency, bandwidth and prefetching set the constant. So the count predicts the shape of the cost, and you measure the rest.
The model needs M and B, and every level of the hierarchy has different ones. Next: how to measure them on the machine in front of you.
